sections.title: Maxwell’s Equations: Electromagnetic Waves Predicted and Observed
objectives: Explain how Maxwell’s equations predict that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field and vice versa.
Describe how Hertz confirmed the existence of electromagnetic waves.

misconceptions.claim: Electromagnetic waves need a medium to travel through.
misconceptions.correction: They do not. They are a changing electric and magnetic field that travel through empty space.

summary: Electromagnetic waves consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields and propagate at the speed of light c . They were predicted by Maxwell, who also showed that c =1μ0ε0,where μ0 is the permeability of free space and ε0 is the permittivity of free space.
Maxwell’s prediction of electromagnetic waves resulted from his formulation of a complete and symmetric theory of electricity and magnetism, known as Maxwell’s equations.

These four equations are paraphrased in this text, rather than presented numerically, and encompass the major laws of electricity and magnetism. First is Gauss’s law for electricity, second is Gauss’s law for magnetism, third is Faraday’s law of induction, including Lenz’s law, and fourth is Ampere’s law in a symmetric formulation that adds another source of magnetism—changing electric fields.

authored_exercises.stem: What did Maxwell predict about a changing electric field?
authored_exercises.answer: That it produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.
solution: Faraday had shown that a changing magnetic field induces an electric field.
Maxwell added the symmetrical term: a changing electric field produces a magnetic field.
Together these effects allow an electromagnetic wave to sustain itself.

authored_exercises.stem: Who produced and detected the first electromagnetic waves, and how?
authored_exercises.answer: Hertz, using an oscillating electric spark to generate the waves and a loop with a small gap to detect them.
solution: A spark discharge produced rapidly changing currents.
Those changing currents radiated electromagnetic waves.
A nearby loop picked up the waves and produced a tiny spark across its gap.

authored_exercises.stem: Find the speed of an electromagnetic wave if μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N m²).
Why did the agreement between Maxwell’s predicted speed and the measured speed of light matter?
authored_exercises.answer: It showed that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
solution: Maxwell’s equations predicted a wave speed from electric and magnetic constants.
The predicted value matched the measured speed of light.
That strongly suggested light is an electromagnetic wave.

misconceptions.claim: Electromagnetic waves need a material medium in order to travel.
misconceptions.correction: Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields that propagate through a vacuum. They do not need a medium; that is why light from the Sun reaches the Earth through space.

misconceptions.claim: In an electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic fields oscillate along the direction of travel.
misconceptions.correction: The fields oscillate perpendicular to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel, so the wave is transverse.

summary: Electromagnetic waves are created by oscillating charges (which radiate whenever accelerated) and have the same frequency as the oscillation.
Since the electric and magnetic fields in most electromagnetic waves are perpendicular to the direction in which the wave moves, it is ordinarily a transverse wave.
The strengths of the electric and magnetic parts of the wave are related by EB= c,which implies that the magnetic field B is very weak relative to the electric field E.

authored_exercises.stem: In an electromagnetic wave, what is the angle between the electric field and the magnetic field?
solution: The two fields are perpendicular to each other.
They are also both perpendicular to the direction of travel.

objectives: List three “rules of thumb” that apply to the different frequencies along the electromagnetic spectrum.

misconceptions.claim: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
misconceptions.correction: They do, at about three hundred million metres per second, but their frequency and wavelength differ.

misconceptions.claim: The electromagnetic spectrum is arranged in order of increasing wavelength.
misconceptions.correction: It runs from radio waves to gamma rays, so the frequency increases as the wavelength decreases. The speed of every one of them in vacuum is the same.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the wavelength ordering as an option.

summary: The relationship among the speed of propagation, wavelength, and frequency for any wave is given by vW=fλ, so that for electromagnetic waves, c=fλ,where f is the frequency, λ is the wavelength, and c is the speed of light.
The electromagnetic spectrum is separated into many categories and subcategories, based on the frequency and wavelength, source, and uses of the electromagnetic waves.

Any electromagnetic wave produced by currents in wires is classified as a radio wave, the lowest frequency electromagnetic waves. Radio waves are divided into many types, depending on their applications, ranging up to microwaves at their highest frequencies.

misconceptions.claim: The energy of an electromagnetic wave depends on how bright it is.
misconceptions.correction: The energy of a photon is set by its frequency, $E = hf$. Brightness tells you how many photons arrive, not how much energy each one carries.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the brightness reading as an option.

summary: The energy carried by any wave is proportional to its amplitude squared. For electromagnetic waves, this means intensity can be expressed as Iave=cε0E022,where Iave is the average intensity in W/m2, and E0 is the maximum electric field strength of a continuous sinusoidal wave.
This can also be expressed in terms of the maximum magnetic field strength B0 as I ave = cB 0 2 2μ 0 and in terms of both electric and magnetic fields as Iave=E0B02μ0.
The three expressions for Iave are all equivalent.

sec-3:exr-48.stem: A sinusoidal electromagnetic wave has period $T=3.0×10^{-9}s$ and peak electric field $E_{0}=5.0×10^{5}N/C$. At $t=0$ the electric field has its maximum value. Which of the following is the correct equation for the wave at the antenna?
solution: At $t=0$ the field is a maximum, so the wave is a cosine. Its angular frequency is $2π/T$, giving $E=(5.0×10^{5}N/C)\cos(2πt/T)$ .

sec-3:exr-52.stem: In Hertz's spark-gap experiment, a spark in the transmitting loop sends a pulse to a receiving loop. How do the sparks induced in the receiving loop compare with the spark in the transmitting loop?
solution: (d). The receiving loop captures only part of the energy radiated by the transmitting loop, so the induced spark is weaker.
How much weaker depends on the tuning: when the loops resonate at the same frequency, the transfer is most efficient.
